extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, editors, and people interested in literary publishing and gatekeeping
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/argument about how societies and publishing systems choose who becomes a writer, focusing on how submission systems, scale, and networks privilege certain kinds of work. Offers criteria and structural prescriptions (e.g., regional selection) to surface complex art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader imaginative involvement (Conroy scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifies genres by the percentage of imaginative involvement required from the reader: 'pulp fiction... 20%,' 'ideal literary fiction... around 50%,' and 'difficult fiction... up to 80%.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that require high imaginative involvement need generous, attentive readers to 'bring the story to life.' In high-volume submission contexts, readers skim and such works fail to become the 'living story' they need to be. Use Conroy's scale to anticipate how much sustained attention a piece requires and whether your submission system can supply that attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention/close reading requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stories and poems require a 'quality of attentive engagement' to come alive and cannot be fairly judged by skim-reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If selection processes force skimming (hundreds of manuscripts a day), pieces that need close reading will be misread or ignored. Anti-pattern: expecting equitable evaluation of complex work in a high-volume slush environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity favored by large slush piles
rubrics_metrics.description: The slush-pile model privileges the simple at the expense of the complex; oversimplified tropes and forms come to dominate contemporary prose and poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and selection systems that can only skim will tend to choose work that reads quickly and clearly on first pass (e.g., 'MFA fiction,' 'trauma plots'). To elevate complex work, design smaller-scale or specially attentive evaluation channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and submission volume as a structural evaluator
rubrics_metrics.description: When readers are tasked to read hundreds or thousands of submissions, reading quality and the nature of selection change (a 'phase change' from evaluating a few to evaluating many).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High volume (example figures in essay: 200 → 2,000 → 14,000) erodes the ability to give each piece adequate attention. Systems should limit applicant pools or create staged review processes to avoid the skimming problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connections/nepotism as an (imperfect) functional filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, nepotism and personal connections allowed complex or unconventional works to bypass slush piles and receive close attention from gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While nepotism is inequitable and indefensible, it served the function of compelling gatekeepers to 'look closely.' The essay argues for finding equitable mechanisms that replicate that function without privileging the well-connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/regional gatekeeping as a solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes more regional/localized institutions (e.g., county-specific MFAs, powerful regional journals) that limit applicant pools and act as 'farm teams' to surface talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional models shrink the denominator and make close evaluation feasible; they restrict eligibility geographically (an example: county-only MFAs) and recommend national outlets select from those strong local scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical presence/audition requirement helps selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Theater auditions require physical presence and therefore naturally reduce scale and improve evaluative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous mechanisms in writing (forms of in-person or locally mediated assessment) could similarly reduce the pool and allow more attentive selection. Anti-pattern: fully-remote, anonymous mass submission portals that invite skimming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of publishing power increases slush problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry consolidation (few large publishers, agents mediating access, MFAs mediating access to agents) centralizes submission portals and increases the volume each gate must handle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized portals concentrate the slush and make close reading harder; decentralization or more local institutions might counteract this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for familiarly readable work under constrained attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers under time/volume pressure tend to prefer work they already know how to read; poems or stories that match a reader's prior interpretive habits are advantaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex or formally unusual work is penalized because it requires learning how to read it. Selection systems should ensure some reviewers have the time/interest to learn new modes of reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: MFA credentialism has limited filtering power
rubrics_metrics.description: MFA programs help at later steps but are effective only for a tiny fraction ('top 1%') of applicants; credentialism is not a broad solution to slush problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on MFA credentials as a gate privileges a small subset and doesn't address the larger problem of mass submissions. Systems should not treat MFA as a sufficient proxy for selection at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the denominator small (explicit prescription)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay's explicit prescription: 'we just need more equitable ways of keeping the denominator small' so unusual, complex art can be seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical options include geographically limited programs, regional journals, or staged/localized selection processes. The phrase highlights a design principle: reduce the number of simultaneous items a gate must evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of selection mechanisms shapes biases (analogy to dating apps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass-access platforms change the nature of bias: like Tinder, they make access broad but do not evenly improve chances of selection; different selection systems encode different biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reforming selection systems, consider which biases a given mechanism introduces (e.g., nepotism vs. skimming) and choose structures that minimize unfair exclusion while preserving capacity for close attention.
